reason: The narrative does not support a simple dichotomy of 'regular people wrong, leaders right.' While the text explicitly states that 'the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord' (וַיַּעֲשׂוּ בְנֵי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל הָרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה), the portrayal of leadership is more complex. Gideon, who emerges as the leader God calls, is not depicted as being 'in the right' in any self-assured sense—he repeatedly expresses doubt, fear, and lacks confidence, requiring constant reassurance from God through signs (the fleece test). Moreover, the existing local leaders/elders of the city are shown as misguided, wanting to execute Gideon for destroying the altar of Baal. The story's actual thrust is not about competent leaders versus foolish people, but about a people who have abandoned God's covenant and a reluctant individual who is chosen by God to deliver them—emphasizing divine guidance over human leadership competence.
